New machine. Its objects are: nedupon, letesi, vipevar, teseluk, fotesen, tanesil.
You have 4 tests. Make your first move.

With only 4 tests and an unknown rule, I'll start by testing half the objects to see how the machine reacts.

TEST: nedupon, letesi, vipevar
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

The first three did not light it up. Next I'll test the other three objects to compare.

TEST: teseluk, fotesen, tanesil
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Neither half lit up on its own. So the machine is not simply lighting for any single nexiom. The most likely rule is that it needs both nexioms on it together, which would mean one nexiom is in each half.

That leaves 9 possible pairs, and 2 yes/no tests cannot always tell 9 cases apart, so I'll narrow them as much as I can. This test lights up only if the nexioms are among nedupon/letesi and teseluk/fotesen, which covers 4 of the 9 pairs.

TEST: nedupon, letesi, teseluk, fotesen
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

Assuming the machine lights only when both nexioms are on it, my three tests rule out several pairs:
* Test 1 rules out any pair inside nedupon/letesi/vipevar.
* Test 2 rules out any pair inside teseluk/fotesen/tanesil.
* Test 3 rules out any pair inside nedupon/letesi/teseluk/fotesen.

Five pairs remain: nedupon+tanesil, letesi+tanesil, vipevar+teseluk, vipevar+fotesen and vipevar+tanesil.

One yes/no test cannot settle five cases, so I'll split them as evenly as I can. This test lights up only for nedupon+tanesil or letesi+tanesil.

TEST: nedupon, letesi, tanesil
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

The last test did not light up either. If the machine lights only when both nexioms are on it, that rules out nedupon+tanesil and letesi+tanesil.

Three pairs remain, and all of them include vipevar:
* vipevar + teseluk
* vipevar + fotesen
* vipevar + tanesil

My tests cannot tell these three apart, so the partner is a guess with about a 1-in-3 chance of being right. This also all depends on the "needs both nexioms" rule, which I inferred rather than confirmed. I'll go with teseluk as the partner.

ANSWER: nexioms = vipevar, teseluk
One last question. If only teseluk were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

**No.** Teseluk was in test 2 (teseluk, fotesen, tanesil) and in test 3, and neither lit up. Under my answer, vipevar is the other nexiom, and it was in neither test. So in test 2, teseluk was effectively alone, because objects that are not nexioms never affect the machine. Teseluk on its own would therefore not light it.

This holds whatever the exact rule is, as long as my answer is correct. It also fits my working rule that the machine needs both nexioms together.

PROBE: no

messages.content:
New machine. Its objects are: lidemo, fekara, kurife, bapanul, paralil, degakon.
You have 4 tests. Make your first move.

The rule for how the machine responds to nexioms is still unknown, so I'll start by testing half of the objects to narrow things down.

TEST: lidemo, fekara, kurife
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

The machine did not light up for lidemo, fekara and kurife, but I still don't know the rule. If one nexiom alone is enough to light it, then the nexioms must be two of bapanul, paralil and degakon. If both nexioms are needed, the first result only tells me they weren't both in that group. Testing a single object helps tell these rules apart. Under the "one is enough" rule, it lights only if degakon is a nexiom. Under the "both needed" rule, it can't light.

TEST: degakon
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

The machine stayed dark for lidemo, fekara and kurife, and for degakon alone. If one nexiom alone lights the machine, the nexioms must be bapanul and paralil. If both nexioms are needed, many pairs are still possible. Testing bapanul and paralil together checks both cases. If it lights, they are almost certainly the nexioms. If it doesn't, the "one is enough" rule is ruled out and they are not the pair.

TEST: bapanul, paralil
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

The machine has never lit up: not for lidemo, fekara and kurife, not for degakon alone, and not for bapanul and paralil together.

**Ruling out "one nexiom is enough":** If one nexiom could light the machine, the first two tests would leave only bapanul and paralil. But that pair didn't light it, so this rule is out.

**If both nexioms are needed:** The pair cannot be two of lidemo, fekara and kurife. It also cannot be bapanul with paralil. That leaves 11 possible pairs:
- one of lidemo, fekara or kurife together with one of bapanul, paralil or degakon (9 pairs), or
- bapanul with degakon, or paralil with degakon (2 pairs).

**Choosing the last test:** One test can't settle 11 options. The best I can do is split them roughly in half. Testing lidemo, fekara, bapanul and degakon together would light the machine for 5 of the 11 pairs:
- lidemo with bapanul
- lidemo with degakon
- fekara with bapanul
- fekara with degakon
- bapanul with degakon

TEST: lidemo, fekara, bapanul, degakon
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

Every test came back dark, so I can't pin down the pair for certain.

- **"One nexiom is enough" is ruled out.** That rule would have left only bapanul and paralil after the first two tests, but that pair didn't light the machine.
- **Under "both needed," six pairs remain.** The last test rules out the 5 pairs it contained. That leaves:
  - lidemo and paralil
  - fekara and paralil
  - kurife and bapanul
  - kurife and paralil
  - kurife and degakon
  - paralil and degakon
- **Picking one.** Kurife and paralil each appear in four of those six pairs, so I'll pick kurife with paralil. This is still essentially a guess, with about a 1-in-6 chance of being right.
- **Another possible rule.** If the machine lights only when exactly one nexiom is present, all four results would point to lidemo and fekara instead.

ANSWER: nexioms = kurife, paralil
One last question. If only kurife were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

I'd say no, though nothing I observed proves it directly.

- **Under the rule I worked from**, the machine lights only when both nexioms are present. A single object can never supply both, so kurife alone would stay dark whether or not it is a nexiom.
- **"One nexiom is enough" is ruled out** by my tests. Kurife being a nexiom under that rule is the only way it would light by itself.
- **Under the alternative "exactly one nexiom" rule**, the results point to lidemo and fekara as the nexioms. Kurife wouldn't be one, so it still wouldn't light.

PROBE: no

Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

Nothing lit with the first three, so I'll test the other three to compare.

TEST: kasiba, sutugos, zetolo
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Neither half lit the machine on its own. If any single nexiom were enough, one half would have lit, so that rule is ruled out. The most likely rule is that the machine lights only when both nexioms are on it together. Under that rule, there is one nexiom in each half, which leaves 9 possible pairs.

Two tests can only separate 4 outcomes, so I can't be certain of the answer. I'll mix objects from both halves to narrow the pairs down as much as possible. If this test lights, the nexioms are one of tadopes/belutan plus one of kasiba/sutugos, which is 4 pairs. If it stays dark, 5 pairs remain.

TEST: tadopes, belutan, kasiba, sutugos
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

The last test lit up. If the rule is that both nexioms must be present, then one nexiom is tadopes or belutan, and the other is kasiba or sutugos. That leaves 4 possible pairs. Other rules can't be fully ruled out, but this is the simplest one that fits all three results.

One test can't separate 4 pairs, so I can't be certain of the answer. I'll test tadopes with both of kasiba and sutugos. If it lights, tadopes is a nexiom; if not, belutan is. Either way, I'll then have to guess between kasiba and sutugos, so I expect a 50% chance of getting the pair right.

TEST: tadopes, kasiba, sutugos
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

That test lit up. If the rule is that both nexioms must be present, then **tadopes is a nexiom**. The other one is **kasiba or sutugos**, and none of my tests tell those two apart. So this is a 50/50 guess. I'm choosing kasiba, with no evidence favoring it over sutugos.

Two caveats:
- **The rule itself is assumed.** "Both nexioms required" is the simplest rule that fits all four results, but I never directly confirmed it.
- **Better tests would have helped.** Two tests can only separate 4 outcomes, and 9 pairs were left after my first two. So my opening split meant the final answer would likely need a guess.

ANSWER: nexioms = tadopes, kasiba
One last question. If only kasiba were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

**Probably not.** Kasiba was on the machine in my second test, together with sutugos and zetolo, and the machine stayed dark. Under the rule I assumed, that both nexioms must be present, one object alone can never light the machine. That holds whether or not kasiba is a nexiom. The same answer follows from any rule where adding objects can't turn the light off.

The caveat is that I never confirmed the rule. An unusual rule where adding objects *can* switch the light off would allow a different answer. My tests didn't rule that out, but nothing I saw suggests it.

PROBE: no

New machine. Its objects are: ridudal, panipa, sepudas, rovofak, lutofi, dodarel.
You have 4 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects to narrow down where the nexioms are.

TEST: ridudal, panipa, sepudas
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

The first test didn't light up, so the nexioms may well both be among the other three objects. However, I don't yet know how the machine responds. It might light for a single nexiom or only when both are present. Testing the remaining three together should confirm whether the nexioms are there before I narrow it down.

TEST: rovofak, lutofi, dodarel
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Neither group lit up, yet the two nexioms must be somewhere among these six objects. So the machine does not light for just any nexiom. The likeliest explanation is that it needs both nexioms present at once, with one in each group. That leaves 9 possible pairs. Two yes/no tests cannot fully separate 9 cases, so I'll split them as evenly as I can. This test takes two objects from each group. If it lights, the pair is among 4 candidates; if not, among the remaining 5.

TEST: ridudal, panipa, rovofak, lutofi
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

Assuming the machine lights only when both nexioms are on it, test 3 ruled out the four pairs drawn only from ridudal/panipa and rovofak/lutofi. That leaves 5 possible pairs:
- sepudas + rovofak
- sepudas + lutofi
- sepudas + dodarel
- ridudal + dodarel
- panipa + dodarel

One yes/no test can't separate 5 cases, so I'll split them as evenly as I can. This test lights for 2 of the pairs (sepudas + rovofak, sepudas + lutofi). If it stays dark, 3 pairs remain. Either way I'll have to make some guess in my answer. This all depends on my assumption about the rule, which fits the results so far but isn't proven.

TEST: sepudas, rovofak, lutofi
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

Assuming the machine lights only when **both** nexioms are on it, here is what the tests show:

- **Test 1** (ridudal, panipa, sepudas) and **test 2** (rovofak, lutofi, dodarel) stayed dark. So the nexioms are split, with one in each group.
- **Test 3** (ridudal, panipa, rovofak, lutofi) stayed dark. This rules out the four pairs drawn only from those objects.
- **Test 4** (sepudas, rovofak, lutofi) lit up. So both nexioms are among these three. Since the pair must include one object from each original group, **sepudas** must be one of them.

The second nexiom is either rovofak or lutofi. My tests can't tell these two apart, so this is a 50/50 guess. My answer also depends on the "needs both" rule, which fits every result but isn't proven.

ANSWER: nexioms = sepudas, rovofak
One last question. If only rovofak were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

**No**, I don't think rovofak alone would light the machine.

- **The "needs both" rule fits every result.** Under it, one object can never light the machine, even if it is a nexiom.
- **Test 2 already put rovofak on the machine without lighting it.** That test (rovofak, lutofi, dodarel) stayed dark. Removing lutofi and dodarel should not make it light, unless the rule depends on something odder than which nexioms are present.
- **I checked the main alternative and ruled it out.** I tested whether the machine could instead light only when exactly one nexiom is present. No pair of objects fits all four results under that rule, which makes me more confident in "needs both."

This is still an inference rather than something I tested directly, so it isn't certain.

PROBE: no
